concepts.def: Change in the heritable characteristics of a population over generations. The unit that evolves is the population, not the individual: the frequencies of alleles, and therefore of the heritable characteristics they determine, change from one generation to the next. Characteristics acquired during an organism's lifetime and not genetic in origin are not passed on, so changes in them are not regarded as evolution.

A feature that develops in an individual during its lifetime as a result of its activities or environment, such as enlarged muscles from training, a suntan or a learned skill. Acquired characteristics are not genetic in origin and are not inherited, so a change in them, however widespread in a population, is not evolution.

The pre-Darwinian idea that characteristics acquired by an organism during its life through use or disuse of its organs are passed on to its offspring, so that a species changes by inheriting acquired characteristics. Defining evolution as change in heritable characteristics distinguishes Darwinian evolution from Lamarckism, because acquired changes that are not genetic in origin cannot be inherited.

In science, a well-supported explanation that predicts and explains a broad range of observations. The theory of evolution by natural selection is unlikely ever to be falsified, but the nature of science makes it impossible to prove formally that it is true by correspondence with every fact. It is therefore accepted as a pragmatic truth and still called a theory, despite all the supporting evidence; the word does not mean a guess or an untested idea.

Evidence for evolution obtained by comparing the base sequences of DNA or RNA, or the amino acid sequences of proteins, in different species. Differences in a sequence accumulate over time after two lineages split from a common ancestor, so species with fewer sequence differences share a more recent common ancestor than species with more differences. The pattern of similarity across many species matches a branching tree of descent, which gives powerful evidence of common ancestry.

A species from which two or more later species are descended. Living species are not the ancestors of other living species: two present-day species that share many features or sequences do so because both inherited them from the same ancestral population that lived in the past.

The deliberate choice by humans of which individuals of a domesticated animal or crop plant are allowed to breed, based on the heritable characteristics wanted. Repeated over generations it changes the heritable characteristics of the population, so it is evolution driven by artificial rather than natural selection. The breeder does not create the variation but selects among the heritable variation already present, including new mutations.

A population of a domesticated animal species (a breed) or crop plant species (a variety) that differs in heritable characteristics from other populations of the same species because of selective breeding. The differences between breeds and varieties, and between them and the original wild species (such as the differences between dog breeds and the grey wolf, or between cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi and Brussels sprouts and wild cabbage, Brassica oleracea), show how rapidly evolutionary change can occur; the breeds and varieties remain members of one species.

Structures in different species that are similar because they were inherited from a common ancestor, even if they now perform different functions. Their shared underlying pattern is not explained by function, since each could have been built differently, but is explained by descent with modification from the same ancestral structure, so homologous structures are evidence for evolution.

The limb pattern shared by amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals: a single bone in the upper limb, two bones in the lower limb, a group of wrist or ankle bones, and five digits each made of a series of small bones. The human arm, the wing of a bat, the flipper of a whale and the leg of a horse are all pentadactyl limbs adapted to different functions, so they are homologous structures inherited from a common ancestor.

Structures in different species that have the same function but different evolutionary origins. They resemble each other because similar selection pressures favoured similar solutions, not because they were inherited from a common ancestor. Examples include the wings of insects and of birds, and the streamlined bodies and fins of sharks and dolphins.

The independent evolution of similar features in species that are not closely related, because they live in similar environments or have similar ways of life and experience similar selection pressures. Convergent evolution is the origin of analogous structures; the species remain separate and do not become more closely related to each other.

The splitting of a pre-existing species into two or more species that can no longer interbreed. This is the only way in which new species have appeared, so each speciation event increases the total number of species on Earth. Gradual evolutionary change within a single species, without splitting, is not speciation.

The disappearance of a species when its last member dies. Extinction decreases the total number of species on Earth, while speciation increases it, so the number of species alive at any time is the outcome of these two processes.

The absence of interbreeding between two populations, so that alleles cannot pass between their gene pools. It is the starting condition for speciation: while gene flow continues, differences that arise in one population spread to the other, but once populations are reproductively isolated they can diverge until they are separate species.

Different selection pressures acting on two reproductively isolated populations, for example because their environments, food sources or competitors differ, so that different heritable characteristics are favoured in each. Over generations the populations diverge, and if divergence continues they become unable to interbreed. Bonobos, living south of the Congo River, and common chimpanzees, living north of it, diverged from one ancestral population in this way after the river separated them: neither species swims, and conditions on the two sides differ, for example bonobos have no gorillas competing for food in their range.

Separation of populations by a physical barrier such as a river, a mountain range or a stretch of sea that members of the species cannot cross. It is one means of achieving reproductive isolation: the Congo River separates bonobos from common chimpanzees because neither species swims.

Speciation in which the populations that diverge are in different places, having been reproductively isolated by a geographical barrier. Once gene flow has stopped, differential selection in the two areas causes the gene pools to diverge until the populations can no longer interbreed.

Speciation in which the diverging populations live in the same area. Reproductive isolation is achieved without a geographical barrier, for example by behavioural isolation, by temporal isolation, or in plants by polyploidy. As in allopatric speciation, reproductive isolation prevents gene flow and the gene pools then diverge.

Reproductive isolation caused by differences in behaviour, particularly courtship: individuals only mate with partners whose courtship signals, such as song, display or scent, are those of their own group, so populations sharing an area do not interbreed.

Reproductive isolation caused by differences in the timing of reproduction, such as flowering, mating or spawning at different times of the day or year, so that populations sharing the same area cannot interbreed. It refers to timing within the lives of present-day organisms, not to living in different periods of Earth's history.

The rapid diversification of a single ancestral species into many species, each adapted to a different niche, typically where vacant niches are available, for example after colonization of an island group or after an extinction event. Because each species specializes on a different resource or habitat, closely related species can coexist without competing, so adaptive radiation increases biodiversity in the ecosystem.

A role in an ecosystem, defined by the resources, habitat and way of life it involves, that no species currently occupies. Vacant niches remove competition from occupying them, which allows descendants of a colonizing species to specialize in different ways and is the condition under which adaptive radiation occurs.

An offspring produced by mating between members of two different species, such as a mule, which is the offspring of a horse and a donkey. Hybrids are usually rare because barriers such as differences in courtship behaviour prevent mating, and when they are produced they are usually sterile, so alleles do not mix between the gene pools of the two species.

The inability of an interspecific hybrid to produce viable gametes. A horse has 64 chromosomes and a donkey 62, so a mule has 63; the chromosomes inherited from the two parent species are not homologous pairs and cannot all pair up during meiosis, so functional gametes are not formed. The mule is healthy and vigorous but cannot breed, so its horse and donkey alleles reach no further generation.

Species-specific signals such as songs, displays, colours or scents that precede mating and are recognized only by members of the same species. Because individuals do not respond to the courtship of another species, courtship behaviour often prevents hybridization in animals, so it acts as a barrier that keeps the alleles of different species from mixing.

Possession of more than two complete sets of chromosomes in each cell. In plants, a sterile hybrid between two species can become fertile if its chromosome number doubles, because every chromosome then has a homologous partner to pair with in meiosis. The polyploid cannot produce fertile offspring with either parent species, so it is reproductively isolated from both and is a new species.

The formation of a new species in a single generation rather than by gradual divergence over many generations. In plants it occurs by hybridization between two species followed by polyploidy: the fertile polyploid hybrid is immediately isolated from both parent species. The knotweeds or smartweeds, genus Persicaria, contain many species that have been formed by these processes.

mcqs.q: Which of these changes would a biologist regard as evolution?
options: The frequency of an allele for dark wing colour rises in a moth population over many generations.
The muscles a weightlifter enlarges by training are inherited by the weightlifter's children.
An individual Arctic fox grows a thicker and whiter coat each year as winter approaches.
Young chimpanzees learn from adults how to crack nuts with stones, and the skill spreads.
mcqs.specStatementText: Evolution is heritable change in a population, and why it is still called a theory
mcqs.explain: Evolution is change in the heritable characteristics of a population. A rise in the frequency of an allele across generations is exactly such a change, whatever the cause of the selection.
rationales: Evolution is change in the heritable characteristics of a population. A rise in the frequency of an allele across generations is exactly such a change, whatever the cause of the selection.

A student who accepts the Lamarckian idea that acquired characteristics are inherited picks this. Enlarged muscles are acquired during life and are not genetic in origin, so they cannot be inherited and no evolution results.

A student who thinks an individual evolves when it changes during its life picks this. The fox's seasonal coat is a response by one individual, not a change in the heritable characteristics of a population.
A student who counts anything handed down from parents to offspring as heritable picks this. A learned skill spreads by imitation, not through alleles, so its spread is not evolution.

mcqs.q: A student says: 'Evolution by natural selection is only a theory, so it has not been proved and could easily be overturned.' Which response best evaluates this claim?
options: The claim is right: a scientific theory is just an untested idea, and evolution will become a fact once enough evidence has been gathered.
The theory cannot be formally proved true, but it predicts and explains so many observations that it is unlikely ever to be falsified.
The claim is wrong because the theory has been proved true by direct observation of every prediction that it makes.
The claim is right because the theory only describes past events, which cannot be tested by scientific experiment.
mcqs.specStatementText: Evolution is heritable change in a population, and why it is still called a theory
mcqs.explain: This is the nature-of-science position in the guide: no theory can be proved true by correspondence, so evolution remains a theory, but it is a pragmatic truth supported by a broad range of observations and is unlikely ever to be falsified.
rationales: A student who uses the everyday meaning of 'theory' picks this. In science a theory is a well-supported explanation; evolution stays a theory not because evidence is lacking but because science cannot formally prove any theory true.

This is the nature-of-science position in the guide: no theory can be proved true by correspondence, so evolution remains a theory, but it is a pragmatic truth supported by a broad range of observations and is unlikely ever to be falsified.

A student who believes science proves its theories picks this. No finite set of observations can prove a theory true for all cases; the theory of evolution is accepted as a pragmatic truth, not a proved one.

A student who thinks only directly observed events can be tested picks this. The theory makes predictions about present-day sequence data, homologous structures and selective breeding, and these predictions have been tested repeatedly.

mcqs.q: The amino acid sequence of the same protein was compared in four species. Compared with species W, species X differs at 2 positions, species Y at 15 positions and species Z at 31 positions. Which conclusion is supported by the data?
options: Z is the most primitive of the four species, because its sequence is furthest from W's.
X lives in the same kind of habitat as W, because similar conditions give similar proteins.
W shares a more recent common ancestor with X than it does with either Y or Z.
X is the ancestor of W, because the two sequences are almost identical.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sequence similarity is evidence of common ancestry
mcqs.explain: Differences in amino acid sequence accumulate over time after two lineages split from a common ancestor. W and X differ least, so their common ancestor is the most recent; Z, with the most differences, diverged from W earliest.
rationales: A student who reads sequence differences as a ranking from primitive to advanced picks this. Differences accumulate in both lineages after they split, so 31 differences means W and Z diverged longest ago, not that Z is primitive.

A student who thinks the environment shapes sequences picks this. Sequence similarity is inherited from a common ancestor; similar habitats produce convergent features, not similar amino acid sequences.

Differences in amino acid sequence accumulate over time after two lineages split from a common ancestor. W and X differ least, so their common ancestor is the most recent; Z, with the most differences, diverged from W earliest.

A student who pictures living species as ancestors of other living species picks this. Both W and X are present-day species descended from the same ancestral population; the near-identical sequence shows a recent split, not descent of one from the other.

mcqs.q: For one gene, two species have identical amino acid sequences in the protein, yet the base sequences of the gene differ at six positions. Which statement explains this?
options: They are not evidence of divergence, because they have had no effect on the protein.
The genes must actually be identical, so the six differences are sequencing errors.
Similar environments keep the proteins alike while the DNA of each species drifts apart.
Some base substitutions leave the amino acid that is coded for unchanged.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sequence similarity is evidence of common ancestry
mcqs.explain: The genetic code is degenerate: several codons code for the same amino acid, so a base substitution can leave the amino acid sequence unchanged. This is why base sequences reveal more differences between species than protein sequences do.
rationales: A student who counts only changes that alter the phenotype picks this. The six base substitutions arose by mutation after the lineages split, so they are evidence of divergence whether or not they alter the protein.

A student who believes every base change alters the protein picks this. Several codons specify the same amino acid, so base substitutions can occur without changing the amino acid sequence; no error need be involved.

A student who thinks the environment shapes sequences picks this. The protein is identical because the genetic code is degenerate, so the six base substitutions do not change any amino acid; similar habitats produce convergent features, not conserved sequences.

The genetic code is degenerate: several codons code for the same amino acid, so a base substitution can leave the amino acid sequence unchanged. This is why base sequences reveal more differences between species than protein sequences do.

mcqs.q: Cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi and Brussels sprouts were all produced from wild cabbage (Brassica oleracea) by selective breeding over the past few thousand years. What does this show about evolution?
options: The heritable characteristics of a population can change greatly in a short time when selection is strong.
Breeders were able to produce each new characteristic by causing the mutation that was needed for it.
It is not evidence of evolution, because the changes were brought about by humans rather than by nature.
Each variety has now become a separate species, because the varieties differ so much in their appearance.
mcqs.specStatementText: Selective breeding shows how fast heritable change can happen
mcqs.explain: Variation between crop varieties, and between them and the original wild species, shows how rapidly evolutionary change can occur. Selective breeding changed the heritable characteristics of these populations within a few thousand years.
rationales: Variation between crop varieties, and between them and the original wild species, shows how rapidly evolutionary change can occur. Selective breeding changed the heritable characteristics of these populations within a few thousand years.

A student who thinks breeders manufacture the features they want picks this. Breeders cannot cause a particular mutation; they select among the heritable variation already present, generation after generation.

A student who treats 'natural' as part of the definition of evolution picks this. Evolution is change in the heritable characteristics of a population; selective breeding produces such change, and its speed is what makes it evidence.
A student who defines species by appearance picks this. All the varieties remain members of Brassica oleracea; they are not reproductively isolated from each other, so no speciation has occurred.

mcqs.q: The arm of a human, the wing of a bat and the flipper of a whale are used for grasping, flying and swimming, yet each has one upper bone, two lower bones, a group of wrist bones and five digits. Why is this evidence for evolution?
options: Five digits is the best possible arrangement for any limb, so each of the species evolved the pattern separately.
The shared bone pattern was inherited from a common ancestor and has been modified for different functions.
The limbs are analogous structures, which show that different functions evolve from different origins.
Bats and whales are older species than humans, so they are our ancestors and passed the pattern on.
mcqs.specStatementText: Homologous structures share an origin, not a function
mcqs.explain: The pentadactyl limb is a homologous structure. The same underlying pattern in limbs with different functions is explained by descent with modification from a common ancestor, not by the demands of grasping, flying or swimming.
rationales: A student who explains every structure by function picks this. A whale has no use for separate digits, and a paddle or a wing could be built in many ways; the shared pattern is inherited, not required by function.

The pentadactyl limb is a homologous structure. The same underlying pattern in limbs with different functions is explained by descent with modification from a common ancestor, not by the demands of grasping, flying or swimming.
A student who has swapped the two terms picks this. Analogous structures have the same function but different origins; these limbs share an origin and differ in function, so they are homologous.

A student who thinks living species are the ancestors of other living species picks this. Humans, bats and whales are all descended from a common ancestor that had the pentadactyl limb; none of the living species is the ancestor of another.

mcqs.q: Sharks, which are fish, and dolphins, which are mammals, both have streamlined bodies, a dorsal fin and paddle-shaped front fins. Which statement about these features is correct?
options: They are homologous, showing that dolphins are more closely related to sharks than they are to other mammals.
They are homologous, because in both animals the features perform the same function in water.
They are analogous: they evolved separately because similar selection favoured similar shapes in water.
They show that the two species are converging on each other and will eventually merge into a single species.
mcqs.specStatementText: Analogous structures come from convergent evolution
mcqs.explain: Analogous structures have the same function but different evolutionary origins. Fish and mammals acquired streamlined bodies and fins independently, by convergent evolution under the similar selection pressures of fast movement through water.
rationales: A student who reads any resemblance as kinship picks this. Dolphins are mammals and share a far more recent common ancestor with other mammals; the resemblance to sharks arose independently.
A student who has swapped the definitions picks this. Same function with different origins is the definition of analogous structures; homologous structures share an origin regardless of function.

Analogous structures have the same function but different evolutionary origins. Fish and mammals acquired streamlined bodies and fins independently, by convergent evolution under the similar selection pressures of fast movement through water.
A student who takes 'converge' to mean the lineages come together picks this. Convergent evolution makes features similar, not species; sharks and dolphins remain as distantly related as they were.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of speciation?
options: A species changes gradually over millions of years until it looks quite different from its ancestors.
A river splits a population into two halves, which are at once regarded as separate species.
An individual is born with a mutation that makes it different from all others of its species.
A population splits into two groups that then become unable to interbreed with each other.
mcqs.specStatementText: New species only ever come from splitting old ones
mcqs.explain: Speciation is the splitting of a pre-existing species into two or more species that can no longer interbreed. It is the only way in which new species have appeared.
rationales: A student who thinks enough change turns a species into a new one picks this. Gradual evolutionary change within one lineage is evolution but is not speciation, because no splitting occurs and no additional species results.

A student who takes geographical separation to be the whole of speciation picks this. The river only stops gene flow; the halves become separate species only if differential selection then makes them diverge until they can no longer interbreed.

A student who thinks a single mutant individual is a new species picks this. Speciation is the splitting of a population into groups that can no longer interbreed; the mutant is still a member of its parents' species and can breed with them.
Speciation is the splitting of a pre-existing species into two or more species that can no longer interbreed. It is the only way in which new species have appeared.

mcqs.q: Over a period of time, 40 speciation events and 25 extinctions were recorded in a group of organisms. Over the same period several other species in the group changed gradually without splitting. What happened to the number of species in the group?
options: It rose by 15, because only the splitting of species adds to the total and only extinction removes from it.
It rose by more than 15, because the species that changed gradually also became new species.
It fell by 25, because each speciation changes an existing species rather than adding one.
It stayed the same, because in nature each speciation event is balanced by the extinction of a species.
mcqs.specStatementText: New species only ever come from splitting old ones
mcqs.explain: Each speciation event adds one species by splitting one into two, and each extinction removes one: 40 - 25 = 15. Gradual change without splitting is not speciation and does not alter the count.
rationales: Each speciation event adds one species by splitting one into two, and each extinction removes one: 40 - 25 = 15. Gradual change without splitting is not speciation and does not alter the count.

A student who counts gradual change as speciation picks this. A species that changes without splitting remains one species, so it adds nothing to the total; only the 40 splits and 25 extinctions count.
A student who thinks speciation replaces the old species with a new one picks this. Speciation is splitting, so one species becomes two and the total rises by one at each event.
A student who believes the number of species is held in balance picks this. Speciation and extinction are independent processes; here 40 additions and 25 losses give a net increase of 15.

mcqs.q: Bonobos live south of the Congo River and common chimpanzees live north of it; neither species swims. How did the two species arise from one ancestral population?
options: Apes on each side of the river developed the features they needed to survive there and passed them on to their offspring.
The river prevented interbreeding, and different selection pressures on each side caused the populations to diverge.
The river caused mutations to occur that made the apes on each side of it different from one another.
Separation by the river was on its own enough to turn the two populations into two separate species.
mcqs.specStatementText: Isolation starts speciation; differential selection completes it
mcqs.explain: The Congo River gave geographical, and therefore reproductive, isolation. Conditions on the two sides differ, for example in food supply and competitors, so differential selection made the isolated gene pools diverge until they became separate species.
rationales: A student who accepts inheritance of acquired characteristics picks this. Features developed during an individual's life are not inherited; the populations diverged because selection favoured different alleles on the two sides.

The Congo River gave geographical, and therefore reproductive, isolation. Conditions on the two sides differ, for example in food supply and competitors, so differential selection made the isolated gene pools diverge until they became separate species.

A student who thinks the environment directs mutation picks this. Mutations arise at random; the river stopped gene flow, and differential selection on existing variation on each side caused the divergence.

A student who takes isolation to be the whole of speciation picks this. Isolation stopped gene flow, but the populations became separate species only because differential selection then made them diverge.

mcqs.q: A population of lizards was split when rising sea level cut off an island from the mainland. Many generations later, island and mainland lizards can no longer produce fertile offspring together. Which statement about this speciation is correct?
options: Separation was enough by itself, and the two populations were different species as soon as they were cut off.
The populations only became different species once the lizards began to look different from one another.
Separation stopped gene flow, so selection on each side could change the two gene pools independently.
Lizards on the island developed the features they needed and then passed them on to their young.
mcqs.specStatementText: Isolation starts speciation; differential selection completes it
mcqs.explain: Geographical isolation achieved reproductive isolation, ending gene flow between the populations. Differential selection on the island and the mainland then changed the two gene pools in different directions until the lizards could no longer interbreed.
rationales: A student who equates isolation with speciation picks this. When the sea rose the two groups were still one species; they became separate species only after generations of divergence.

A student who defines species by appearance picks this. The test is reproductive isolation: the populations are separate species because they can no longer produce fertile offspring, whatever they look like.

Geographical isolation achieved reproductive isolation, ending gene flow between the populations. Differential selection on the island and the mainland then changed the two gene pools in different directions until the lizards could no longer interbreed.

A student who accepts Lamarckian inheritance picks this. Features developed during life are acquired and not inherited; the island population changed because selection altered allele frequencies over generations.

mcqs.q: Two populations of a fly species live in the same orchard but lay their eggs on different fruit species, which ripen at different times, so the flies rarely mate with each other. Which type of speciation could this lead to, and why?
options: Allopatric speciation, because the two kinds of fruit tree act as a geographical barrier between the populations.
Neither, because temporal isolation refers to species that lived at different times in Earth's history.
Neither, because populations that share the same habitat are bound to interbreed and cannot separate.
Sympatric speciation, because temporal isolation is cutting gene flow with no geographical barrier.
mcqs.explain: The populations occupy the same area, so any speciation is sympatric. Mating at different times is temporal isolation, one of the forms of reproductive isolation that can allow gene pools sharing a habitat to diverge.
rationales: A student who looks for a physical barrier in every example picks this. The flies share the same orchard and can reach each other; the barrier is timing, not geography, so any speciation would be sympatric.
A student who attaches 'temporal' to geological time picks this. Temporal isolation is a difference in the timing of reproduction between present-day populations, exactly as in these flies.

A student who thinks only physical separation can stop gene flow picks this. Reproductive isolation can be temporal: flies that mate at different times do not interbreed even though they live together.

The populations occupy the same area, so any speciation is sympatric. Mating at different times is temporal isolation, one of the forms of reproductive isolation that can allow gene pools sharing a habitat to diverge.

mcqs.q: What do allopatric speciation and sympatric speciation have in common?
options: Both require reproductive isolation of the populations, so that their gene pools can diverge.
Both require a physical barrier, though in sympatric speciation the barrier is very small.
Both require the populations to live in separate areas at some stage in the process.
Both are complete as soon as the populations stop interbreeding, before any genetic change.
mcqs.explain: In both, gene flow between the populations must stop; this reproductive isolation is geographic in allopatric speciation and behavioural or temporal in sympatric speciation. Once isolated, the gene pools diverge until the populations cannot interbreed.
rationales: In both, gene flow between the populations must stop; this reproductive isolation is geographic in allopatric speciation and behavioural or temporal in sympatric speciation. Once isolated, the gene pools diverge until the populations cannot interbreed.
A student who models all speciation on the allopatric example picks this. Sympatric speciation occurs without any physical barrier; isolation is achieved by differences in behaviour or timing.
A student who thinks populations sharing an area cannot stop interbreeding picks this. Sympatric speciation takes place entirely within one area.

A student who takes isolation to be the whole of speciation picks this. Reproductive isolation is the starting condition; the populations become separate species only after their gene pools have diverged.

mcqs.q: A single species of finch colonized a remote group of islands that had no other land birds. Its descendants now form many species, each with a beak suited to a different food. Which statement explains this?
options: This is convergent evolution, because unrelated birds reaching the islands evolved similar beaks.
Vacant niches let the descendants diversify, and specializing on different foods lets the species coexist.
The finches developed the beaks they needed for each food and passed those beaks on to their offspring.
The species must each live on a separate island, because related species cannot share an area without conflict.
mcqs.explain: With no other land birds present, food niches were vacant. Adaptive radiation filled them: each species became adapted to a different food, so closely related species coexist without competing, increasing the biodiversity of the islands.
rationales: A student who conflates the two terms picks this. The species all descend from one colonizing species and have become more different from each other, which is divergence in an adaptive radiation, the opposite of convergence.

With no other land birds present, food niches were vacant. Adaptive radiation filled them: each species became adapted to a different food, so closely related species coexist without competing, increasing the biodiversity of the islands.
A student who accepts inheritance of acquired characteristics picks this. Beak shape did not change by use; selection on each food source favoured birds whose heritable beak shape suited it.
A student who applies competitive exclusion to all related species picks this. Species adapted to different foods occupy different niches, so several can coexist on one island without competing.

mcqs.q: A horse has 64 chromosomes and a donkey has 62. A mule, their hybrid, is healthy and vigorous but almost always sterile. Why is the mule sterile?
options: It has only half of the horse's genes and half of the donkey's, so it lacks a complete set of instructions.
Horses and donkeys must be the same species, so the sterility is a result of inbreeding.
Its 63 chromosomes cannot all pair up during meiosis, so it does not form viable gametes.
A hybrid is an unnatural mixture, so its body rejects the combination of horse and donkey genes.
mcqs.specStatementText: Barriers and sterile hybrids keep gene pools apart
mcqs.explain: The mule inherits 32 chromosomes from the horse and 31 from the donkey. These are not homologous pairs, so pairing in meiosis fails and functional gametes are not produced, even though the animal itself is vigorous.
rationales: A student who thinks a hybrid is made from two incomplete halves picks this. The mule has a complete haploid set from each parent, which is why it develops into a healthy animal; the sets simply cannot pair in meiosis.

A student who thinks producing offspring makes two organisms one species picks this. Horses and donkeys are separate species; the mule's sterility is the mechanism that keeps their alleles from mixing.

The mule inherits 32 chromosomes from the horse and 31 from the donkey. These are not homologous pairs, so pairing in meiosis fails and functional gametes are not produced, even though the animal itself is vigorous.
A student who regards hybrids as defective picks this. The stem states that the mule is healthy and vigorous; its sterility is a failure of chromosome pairing in meiosis, not of its body.

mcqs.q: Two closely related bird species live in the same forest. The males of each species sing a different song, and females respond only to the song of their own species. What is the significance of this for the two species?
options: It is not a barrier to hybridization, because only physical differences can stop two species breeding.
It lets the two species coexist by preventing them from competing with each other for food.
It shows that they are really one species, because they are so alike and live in the same forest.
It prevents hybridization, so that alleles do not pass between the two gene pools.
mcqs.specStatementText: Barriers and sterile hybrids keep gene pools apart
mcqs.explain: Species-specific courtship is a barrier to hybridization. Because females respond only to their own species' song, the two species do not interbreed, and their alleles remain in separate gene pools even though they share a habitat.
rationales: A student who thinks barriers must be physical picks this. Courtship behaviour often prevents hybridization in animals; a song that the other species does not respond to is an effective barrier, and no physical difference is needed.
A student who confuses reproductive barriers with niche separation picks this. Song has nothing to do with feeding; its significance is that it prevents interbreeding.

A student who defines species by appearance picks this. Species are defined by reproductive isolation: the song difference keeps the two gene pools apart, so they are separate species however alike they look and wherever they live.

Species-specific courtship is a barrier to hybridization. Because females respond only to their own species' song, the two species do not interbreed, and their alleles remain in separate gene pools even though they share a habitat.

mcqs.q: Suppose one Persicaria species has 20 chromosomes in each diploid cell and another has 24. A hybrid forms between them, and in one hybrid plant the chromosome number doubles. Which statement is correct?
options: The doubled plant has 44 chromosomes, can pair them all in meiosis, and is a new species isolated from both parents.
The doubled plant remains sterile, because its chromosomes still come from two different species.
The doubled plant is still the same species as its parents, because it can breed with either of them.
The doubled plant dies, because carrying extra sets of chromosomes is lethal, as it is in human cells.
mcqs.specStatementText: Plants can form new species in one generation
mcqs.explain: The hybrid receives 10 chromosomes from one parent and 12 from the other, 22 in all, which have no homologous partners. Doubling gives 44, so every chromosome has a partner and meiosis works. Crosses with either parent give unbalanced, sterile offspring, so the polyploid is a new species.
rationales: The hybrid receives 10 chromosomes from one parent and 12 from the other, 22 in all, which have no homologous partners. Doubling gives 44, so every chromosome has a partner and meiosis works. Crosses with either parent give unbalanced, sterile offspring, so the polyploid is a new species.

A student who blames sterility on the mixture of species picks this. The hybrid was sterile because its 22 chromosomes had no partners; after doubling each has an identical partner, so pairing and meiosis succeed.

A student who assumes interbreeding with the parents continues picks this. A cross with the 20-chromosome parent gives offspring with 22 + 10 = 32 chromosomes, which cannot pair properly, so the polyploid is reproductively isolated.
A student who generalizes from human chromosome disorders picks this. Polyploidy is common and well tolerated in plants; a complete extra set is balanced, unlike a single extra chromosome.

mcqs.q: A botanist claims that species R of Persicaria arose abruptly by hybridization between species P and species Q, followed by polyploidy. Which observation would best support this claim?
options: R appears in the fossil record after a long series of intermediate forms between P and Q.
The diploid chromosome number of R equals the diploid numbers of species P and Q added together.
R produces fully fertile offspring when crossed with either species P or species Q.
R has fewer chromosomes than either P or Q, as expected for a hybrid with half of each parent's set.
mcqs.specStatementText: Plants can form new species in one generation
mcqs.explain: A hybrid of P and Q has one haploid set from each; doubling gives two sets from each, so the polyploid's diploid number is the sum of the two parents' diploid numbers. This is the signature of speciation by hybridization and polyploidy.
rationales: A student who expects every speciation to be gradual picks this. A polyploid species arises in a single generation, so a long series of intermediates would count against the claim rather than for it.

A hybrid of P and Q has one haploid set from each; doubling gives two sets from each, so the polyploid's diploid number is the sum of the two parents' diploid numbers. This is the signature of speciation by hybridization and polyploidy.

A student who thinks the polyploid can still breed with its parents picks this. Fertile offspring with P would mean R is not reproductively isolated from P, which would count against R being a separate polyploid species.

A student who thinks a hybrid carries only half of each parent's chromosomes picks this. A hybrid has a complete haploid set from each parent, and after polyploidy has twice that, so R should have more chromosomes than either parent, not fewer.
